title: How do firearms seized over mental health concerns get returned, like in the Tumbler Ridge case?
summary: There’s been a lot of debate surrounding the return of seized firearms taken from the home of the Tumbler Ridge shooter, especially after a recent U.S. court filing suggested Jesse Van Rootselaar…

image.caption: A memorial for the victims of a school shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary is pictured on Feb. 11, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

There’s been a lot of debate surrounding the return of seized firearms taken from the home of the Tumbler Ridge shooter, especially after a recent U.S. court filing suggested Jesse Van Rootselaar used those guns in the mass shooting.
RCMP say owner of firearms petitioned courts to get them back. Experts explain how the law works

There’s been a lot of debate surrounding the return of seized firearms taken from the home of the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., shooter, especially after a recent U.S. court filing suggested Jesse Van Rootselaar used those guns in this year's mass shooting.
An American, Melody Bryant, who was charged under her legal name James Cody Bryant, is accused of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

While Canadian media, including CBC News, have been fighting to gain access to court documents in British Columbia, U.S. court filings in the Bryant case have been the main source of information in the Tumbler Ridge massacre.

A motion filed last week by Bryant’s lawyers in an attempt to free their client said the RCMP had removed and returned Van Rootselaar’s guns, one of which had been altered to enable more rapid firing.
"In fact, the RCMP apparently returned the gun with the alteration intact. Van Rootselaar then used the altered firearm in the shooting," the lawyers wrote in a Nov. 18 motion filed in Seattle.

CBC News is part of a media consortium fighting to get access to Canadian court records involving the seizure and return of the firearms from Van Rootselaar’s home. That case is under a publication ban which RCMP say limits their ability to say anything more than what has already been publicly provided.
In 2024, Jennifer Strang, Jesse Van Rootselaar’s mother, posted a photo on social media of a gun safe in her home. (Jennifer Strang/Facebook)

After the Tumbler Ridge shooting, RCMP said in a Feb. 13 news release that a long gun and modified rifle were seized from the school. It said two firearms, including a shotgun, were seized, among a number of other firearms, at the residence.

The shotgun is believed to have been used in the homicides at the home and had not been previously seized by police. Mounties also said they had not previously seized the main firearm used in the school shooting and its origins are unknown.
On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother Jennifer Strang, 39, and half-brother Emmett Jacobs, 11, in their home.

She then drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she gunned down Abel Mwansa, 12, Zoey Benoit, 12, Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Kylie Smith, 12, Ticaria Lampert, 12, and educational assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39.
Two other students were shot but survived.

blocks.text: The next day, RCMP Deputy Commissioner Dwayne McDonald said there was a history of police attending the family residence over the past several years, some of those calls related to mental health issues.
He said RCMP seized firearms from the home years prior and the lawful owner of those firearms petitioned the court to have them returned.

"The individual who petitioned the court would have probably had to show how these firearms would be safely kept away from the individual who poses the public safety concern," said criminal defence lawyer Silvia Badea, who specializes in cases involving the seizure and return of firearms.

She said the Crown would have presented their position on whether or not the firearms should be returned, but ultimately it’s up to a judge to decide if the measures presented by the owner appropriately address the public safety concerns.

"I think what's very difficult is balancing the interests of people. Ultimately, the individual whose weapons are seized that isn't necessarily the individual having the mental health crisis also has a set of rights," said Badea.
Chat records reportedly show how ChatGPT helped Tumbler Ridge shooter

While RCMP have said they had not seized the main firearm used in the school shooting and its origins are unknown, U.S. court records show Van Rootselaar complained to Bryant about an SKS rifle that had been "roughly confiscated" by RCMP that was no longer accurate when it was returned.
While the Canadian court records may reveal which version of events is true, Badea said if a judge decides it’s safe to return the guns to their owner, the RCMP would have to comply.
Badea said a modification that would make a gun "fire more rapidly" as the U.S. court documents state, would likely be illegal.
"I would be very surprised if they [RCMP] were to return something that was fully illegal. I think that obviously everyone could understand how that would be problematic," said Badea.

In the criminal complaint against Bryant, the FBI said Jesse Van Rootselaar sent a photo of herself on the day of the shooting, posing with a firearm. (U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington at Seattle)
Firearms policy expert Noah Schwartz said it is possible police didn’t know the gun had been modified because it would not have been sent to a lab to be disassembled and test fired.
"Which would be how you would detect whether a device like that had been installed," said Schwartz, an assistant professor of political science at the Royal Military College.
He said it’s also possible Van Rootselaar lied about the firearms or installed a device and didn't really know how it worked.

"There's a lot that we don't know about this case at this stage. And we have to be really careful about speculating on an active investigation, especially given that we know that one of the shooter's motivations was notoriety," said Schwartz.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Caroline is a senior reporter with the CBC News National team based in Vancouver.
